Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure, thereby generating warnings that you may have high blood pressure. However, they will not provide you with your actual blood pressure readings.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices can do so, but require periodic calibration with a traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to deliver full blood pressure measurements without any calibration, and says trials involving thousands of people support this claim…

"Silent Killer"

Abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) can both pose significant health risks.

Of the two, hypertension is the most dangerous. It is known as the "silent killer" because it can cause serious and irreversible damage to the arteries, heart and brain without any obvious symptoms. Many people only discover they have the condition after suffering a heart attack or stroke.

Especially for older adults, it is best to monitor blood pressure regularly, and home upper-arm blood pressure monitors are widely available on the market. However, being able to monitor automatically through a fitness device you are already wearing would of course be ideal.

Blood pressure features on Apple Watch

The launch of watchOS 26 enables five Apple Watch models to measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these models will not give you any readings; they will only alert you when possible signs of high blood pressure are detected. Other devices, such as the Oura Ring, work in a similar way.

Some fitness devices can indeed provide actual blood pressure readings, but they need to be calibrated regularly using readings from an upper-arm blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup Vital Signals claims to have developed a smart ring that can measure blood pressure as accurately as a traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitor without any calibration — the Signal Ring.

According to Bloomberg, CEO Tom Moss said he himself nearly died from undiagnosed high blood pressure, which is why he founded the company.

The ring goes on presale later today, with delivery in October, priced at US$399, with no subscription fees required. Real-time blood pressure readings and long-term tracking results will be displayed in a companion app (as shown in the image above).

It is worth noting that the Oura Ring has not yet received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials show that its blood pressure readings for thousands of participants have been accurate.

Interestingly, Moss does not intend to sell this ring to everyone. He says these professional features are best suited for older adults and those assessed by a doctor as being at high risk of high blood pressure — a statement that also implies the Signal Ring may not perform as well as other products in other areas (such as sleep tracking).
